title: Corrective IR Spatial Reconstruction
description: A live six-channel hybrid system combining per-channel corrective FIRs for the initial response with a separately applied target-hall reverberation tail.
question: How closely can electroacoustic correction bring a live venue toward another hall’s early response and reverberant character?
body: I began with a practical problem: applying a target hall impulse response directly in a live venue does not reproduce that hall consistently, because the processed sound still passes through the current venue and accumulates its acoustic response.

For the live system, I measured six loudspeaker-to-microphone paths using a stage-rigged AB microphone pair. A Python pipeline aligned the current and target IRs with GCC-PHAT, then generated a regularized, band-limited corrective FIR for each surround channel. The correction focused on the 125 Hz–4 kHz band and approximately the first 40 ms of the response.

In Max/MSP, each of the six surround channels was convolved with its own corrective FIR. The target hall’s reverberation tail from approximately 200 ms onward was applied separately through Convology XT, while the main PA retained the direct sound and primary mix balance.

At the measurement position centered on the fourth audience row, the mean spectral error against the target hall across all six channels decreased from 2.69 dB to 2.24 dB in the initial 0–40 ms and 125 Hz–4 kHz analysis range. This is a first-stage comparison using the measurements involved in filter generation; it does not establish an equivalent sound field throughout the audience area or a perceptual match to the target hall. Controlled listening evaluation remains future work.

title: Yamaha Sound xR Image Renderer System Identification
description: A black-box measurement study of how Sound xR Image maps loudspeaker geometry, Object position, and renderer parameters to output gains.
question: How does Yamaha Sound xR Image translate spatial coordinates and rendering parameters into loudspeaker gains?
body: This study followed the outdoor Sound xR Image deployment and focused on the renderer itself. I treated the system as a black box, varying loudspeaker coordinates and IDs, Object position, XY mode, Width, Height, Precision, and Distance Attenuation while recording the resulting output gains.

The measurements were compared with numerical candidates while keeping observed values separate from inferred equations. The resulting formulas are bounded explanatory models, not claims about Yamaha’s disclosed internal implementation.

Within clearly documented normal-output regions, inverse-distance weighting followed by constant-power normalization explained the recorded gain distribution. The five Precision settings were consistent with distance exponents corresponding to approximately 8–12 dB of unnormalized attenuation per distance doubling, and representative verified blocks typically matched within about 0.005 dB.

Other behavior remains conditional. Size measurements support candidate effective-distance formulas only within the tested configurations, while boundary projection, Distance Attenuation, Object Z in 3D operation, and changes caused by loudspeaker-ID assignment do not yet reduce to one general rule. Repeated tests ruled out several simpler explanations, including a mere output-column swap.

The current outcome is a bounded renderer model suitable for a Max/MSP prototype, together with a prioritized validation plan. A fully compatible clone for arbitrary layouts, out-of-area positions, and dynamic motion requires further measurements of channel mapping, state application, 3D control paths, smoothing, and time response.

title: Multichannel Spatial Mixing System
description: Exploring immersive sound image control and spatial mixing approaches for small performance venues.
question: How can spatial audio connect what audiences see with what they hear in a performance space?
body: In many live performance environments, conventional stereo sound reinforcement effectively collapses into mono due to strong direct sound from the stage. This makes it difficult to form a stable phantom image, especially for vocals, without deploying a dedicated center speaker.

This project explored an alternative multi-channel spatial mixing approach, aiming to achieve intuitive sound image control by physically aligning the “line of hearing” with the “line of sight.” The system was implemented using a 3.1-channel base structure with additional stage rear speakers, relying solely on the audio console’s routing and bus architecture—without an external immersive processor.

Mixing strategies were designed to separate sound image roles: front-heavy sources (vocals, kick, snare, bass) were routed to a center channel, while harmonic and spatial elements were distributed across LR and stage rear speakers. Spatial effects were used to enhance envelopment rather than primary image formation. System tuning treated the rig as two independent systems, focusing on temporal and spectral alignment rather than full electrical unification. While the setup achieved clear physical separation of sound sources, audience feedback revealed an unexpected result: rather than perceiving a cohesive spatial image, listeners experienced instruments as disconnected sound objects.

This outcome highlighted the limitations of purely physical and electrical approaches to spatial mixing, emphasizing the necessity of psychoacoustic and perception-centered design. The project ultimately reframed spatial mixing as a human-perception problem rather than a purely technical routing challenge.

title: WAN Audio Transmission System
description: Exploring real-time networked audio systems for remote musical interaction and collaboration.
question: How can musical collaboration continue when physical distance becomes a limitation?
body: This project investigated whether real-time, sample-accurate multi-channel audio transmission between DAWs is feasible over a Wide Area Network (WAN), assuming remote performance, recording, or live mixing scenarios.

Multiple approaches were sequentially tested and evaluated, including commercial network audio protocols (AES67, Dante, AVB), server-based relay systems, peer-to-peer transmission methods, and open-source solutions such as ffmpeg, JACK Audio, and JackTrip. While several methods achieved stable network connectivity and acceptable latency, none could guarantee long-term sample accuracy in a WAN environment.

Through systematic experimentation, the study identified that the core limitation was not network bandwidth or latency, but the absence of a shared hardware word clock between geographically separated DAWs. Without a common master clock, sample drift accumulated over time, resulting in XRUNs and audible digital artifacts such as tick noise.

This research confirmed that real-time multi-channel network audio over WAN is fundamentally constrained by system architecture and clock synchronization, rather than transmission performance alone. The findings suggest that future designs must incorporate an independent synchronization mechanism decoupled from the network transport layer.

title: Performer-Tailored Electronic Drums
description: A Max/MSP drum module with velocity zones and sample layers shaped around an individual performer’s dynamic range.
question: How can an electronic drum’s velocity response be reshaped around an individual performer?
body: Fixed velocity mappings do not always match the usable dynamic range or touch of a particular drummer. This project began by rebuilding the relationship between MIDI velocity and sample playback around one performer’s actual striking characteristics.

The Max/MSP patch routes MIDI notes to kick, snare head, rim, side stick, tom, hi-hat, ride, and crash voices. Custom velocity zones select different samples for snare and ride articulations, while incoming velocity scales playback level across the kit. MIDI CC4 controls hi-hat openness, and each voice has its own gain, panning, and output routing for live mixing.

The result is a manually calibrated, performer-tailored drum module rather than an automatically learning adaptive system. Its current mappings demonstrate how velocity response can be tuned for one player; comparisons across performers and controlled listening tests remain future work.

title: Audio-to-MIDI System (Ongoing Research)
description: Exploring an AI-assisted music creation workflow that transforms audio-based musical ideas into editable digital structures, helping musicians create and modify digital music more intuitively.
question: How can musicians move naturally between human expression and digital composition?
body: Many musicians have musical ideas but face technical barriers when translating them into a digital production environment. This project explores an AI-assisted workflow that transforms audio recordings into editable musical structures, allowing artists to generate and refine performance materials more intuitively.

The system analyzes uploaded audio files to extract musical information such as BPM, key, song structure, and lyrics, then generates initial MIDI materials including drums, bass, chords, and other instrumental layers. Through a web-based mini DAW interface, users can edit MIDI patterns, arrange song sections, and create performance resources such as click tracks and cue tracks.
Rather than replacing musicians’ creative decisions, this project investigates how AI can support the transition between human musical expression and digital music creation.

title: Adaptive Monitor System for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Musicians (Ongoing Research)
description: Exploring adaptive monitoring systems based on how Deaf and hard-of-hearing musicians perceive, perform, and interact with music.
question: What happens when musical systems are designed around different ways of hearing?
body: An ongoing project investigating how performers with different hearing conditions experience monitoring, rehearsal, and musical interaction, and exploring adaptive audio systems based on their needs.
